IMiC intervention effects on human milk: online resource Overview This online resource accompanies the manuscript: Nutritional interventions’ impacts on human milk: three trials in low-resource settings (Dailey-Chwalibóg, Mertens et al., 2026). International Milk Composition (IMiC) Consortium. It reports the analytical outputs behind the manuscript in more detail than the printed article can hold: interactive forest and volcano plots, searchable and filterable estimate tables, longitudinal trajectory plots, MILQ-referenced deficiency analyses, BMI-stratified subgroup analyses, reproducible pathway-enrichment results, and the cross-compartment analyses in maternal and infant blood. The online resource has ten numbered sections, preceded by this unnumbered overview and followed by a page recording the R session that produced it. The paper cites Sections 1–8 by number in its Methods, Results, and figure legends. §9 (reproducible pathway and enrichment analyses) holds the full results behind the manuscript’s pathway tables (Tables S2–S7), and §10 (cross-compartment analyses in maternal and infant blood) those behind its cross-compartment tables (Tables S8–S11) and main-text Fig. 6D; the Results cite both as “the online resource”. Table and figure numbers throughout this online resource match the manuscript’s supplementary materials (Tables S1–S11 and Figs. S1–S5). Each trial contributed its own intent-to-treat population, restricted to dyads with at least one HM measurement contributing to IMiC. Primary outcomes are macronutrients and micronutrients; secondary are HMOs and bioactive proteins; tertiary are targeted metabolites (Biocrates MxP Quant 500); exploratory are untargeted metabolomics, untargeted proteomics, and microbiome composition. All components were expressed in native assay units, then standardized to study × visit z-scores before TMLE, so effect estimates on the z-score scale are mean differences in SD units. FDR correction was applied within each outcome group × study × visit. Complete methods are in the manuscript’s Materials and methods. The enrichment and cross-compartment sections use two different mass tolerances, which are not interchangeable. Pathway and compound annotation in §9 (Mummichog) uses a 10 ppm database tolerance against the human_mfn library, whereas cross-platform feature matching in §10 uses a ±25 ppm tolerance between two measured masses (ppm = |m₁ − m₂| / m × 10⁶ ≤ 25). 0.3 How to read interactive figures In the web version, forest and volcano plots are interactive plotly widgets. Hovering over a point shows the component name, study, visit, ATE, 95% CI, and FDR-adjusted Q-value, and the mode bar at the top right of each plot zooms, pans, lasso-selects, or exports a PNG. Each plot is paired with a searchable table of the same data, with column filters and sortable columns. Plots drawn for this online resource use the colorblind-safe Okabe–Ito palette. Significance levels, studies, BMI strata, and randomized contrasts also differ in symbol shape or line type, so the plots can be read with a color-vision deficiency or in grayscale. If a data file that a section depends on is missing, the section prints a notice naming the file in place of its output. Rerunning the analysis code (see Reproducing the online resource in the repository README) regenerates these files. 0.4 Machine-readable data files Four supplementary tables (S1, S3, S6, and S7) were too large to print in full, so the supplementary materials give a short caption for each and point here for the complete data; Table S1 comes in wide and long formats. Section 3 Subgroup analyses stratified by maternal BMI This section examines whether intervention effects on human milk components depended on maternal nutritional status at baseline, using maternal body mass index (BMI) as a marker of that status, dichotomized into underweight (BMI ≤ 18.5 kg/m²) and normal or overweight (BMI > 18.5 kg/m²) strata. We estimated stratum-specific ATEs with the same TMLE framework used in the primary adjusted analyses. Interaction P-values come from a Wald-type test of the difference between the two stratum-specific estimates, divided by the standard error of the difference. The results shown here are the component × study × visit combinations with a nominally significant interaction (all interaction P < 0.01): 129 in Mumta-LW (1.5 and 2 months) and one in MISAME-III (3–4 months); six, all in Mumta-LW, remain significant after FDR correction. The manuscript cites this section as “Section 3 of the online resource” in the Results paragraph on macronutrient and micronutrient effects, where it reports that maternal BMI did not consistently modify macronutrient or micronutrient effects. These subgroup analyses are exploratory and not powered to detect modest interactions, particularly in studies with a small underweight stratum. Differences in the size or direction of per-component estimates between BMI strata should be interpreted cautiously, especially when the 95% CIs are wide. 3.1 Per-component stratified forest plots Figure (online-only). Section 4 Exploratory high-dimensional outcomes: microbiome, untargeted proteomics, untargeted metabolomics This section covers human milk components that were not designated as primary or secondary outcomes: the milk microbiome (α-diversity and individual taxa), untargeted proteomics, and untargeted metabolomics. These analyses survey where intervention-related signals might exist in high-dimensional data and generate hypotheses for follow-up. All of these results call for caution. They carry a heavy multiple-testing burden and variable measurement error, and some rest on small samples or incomplete intervention contrasts. Formal inference and the primary conclusions come from the prespecified primary and secondary outcomes in the Adjusted intervention effects section. Pathway-level interpretation of the metabolomic and proteomic signals, which is easier to read biologically, is in the Pathway enrichment section. The forest and volcano plots in this section are interactive plotly figures; hovering over a point shows the compound or taxon name, study, visit, ATE, and FDR-adjusted Q-value. Each plot has a searchable, filterable table of the same data. For untargeted proteomics (3,001 estimates) and untargeted metabolomics (~97,000 features across studies, visits, and ionization modes, giving 353,656 estimates), the interactive plot shows only the 2,000 and 5,000 estimates with the smallest raw P-values, so that the page stays responsive. The sub-caption of each plot states what its table contains: every feature for the microbiome and proteomics, and the features with Q < 0.10 for untargeted metabolomics. Section 5 Adjusted intervention effects on individual milk components This section reports the primary covariate-adjusted estimates of maternal nutritional intervention effects on individual human milk components. Each component appears in an interactive forest plot and a searchable table, stratified by study and milk collection visit. We estimated average treatment effects (ATEs) with targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE), adjusting for prespecified baseline prognostic factors, and applied Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction within each outcome group × study × visit. Every results table also includes pval_adj_global, a more conservative correction pooled across all studies and visits within an outcome group, which we retain as a sensitivity analysis; the significance flag (sigFDR) is based on the per-visit pval_adj. Each outcome group appears twice. The first view pools the intervention arms (all maternal nutritional intervention arms combined vs. the corresponding control) to maximize precision. The second stratifies by randomized arm, comparing each randomized nutritional arm with its trial’s control. In the forest plots, filled triangles mark effects that survive FDR correction, filled circles (“Sig before FDR”) mark nominal P < 0.05 that did not survive correction, and open circles mark neither; in the arm-stratified plots, each contrast also has its own color and CI line type. Hovering over a point shows the exact estimate, 95% CI, and Q-value, and the column filters in each table narrow the view to specific components, studies, or visits. These estimates correspond to Figure 2 (primary outcomes) of the manuscript and Figure S3 (secondary outcomes) of the supplementary materials, and supply the per-component estimates behind the Figure 5A targeted-metabolite volcano plot. The machine-learning prediction of treatment arm and the PCA composites of manuscript Figure 1 are in §8. Native assay units. Section 6 Targeted-metabolite metadata and reductions in HM nutrient deficiency This section has two parts. The first, Targeted-metabolite metadata, is the inventory of the Biocrates MxP Quant 500 panel cited in the manuscript’s Fig. 5A legend (“metadata are in Section 6 of the online resource”). The randomized comparison is unchanged; only the threshold comes from an external reference population. Section 7 Trajectory analyses of human milk component change across lactation The trajectory analyses in this section ask whether maternal nutritional interventions altered within-individual changes in human milk composition across successive postpartum visits. The cross-sectional analyses elsewhere in this online resource compare arms at a given visit; these track visit-to-visit change within the same mother–infant dyad. Section 10 Cross-compartment analyses in maternal and infant blood This section reports the cross-compartment analyses in the MISAME-III subset with paired maternal plasma, maternal and infant dried-blood microsample (VAMS) metabolomics, and maternal blood proteomics, set alongside the milk measurements analyzed elsewhere in this online resource. The milk analyses in the rest of this online resource (§1–§9) pool all three trials (MISAME-III, Mumta-LW, ELICIT). The blood and cross-compartment analyses here use MISAME-III only, the one trial in which maternal plasma, dried-blood VAMS metabolomics, and blood proteomics were collected. MISAME-III randomized prenatal and postnatal balanced energy-protein (BEP) supplementation in a 2×2 design, giving four arms: Control (IFA/IFA), prenatal-only (BEP/IFA), postnatal-only (IFA/BEP), and both periods (BEP/BEP). The postnatal (lactation-period) contrast is the one of interest, because any effect carried through milk would be expected to appear there in both milk and infant blood. Visit codes. Blood tables use MISAME-III visit codes; milk tables use calendar labels. tri3 = third trimester · incl = enrollment · acco = birth/accouchement · pn12 = 1–2 months postpartum · pn34 = 3–4 months · pn56 = 5–6 months. The text gives months; the data tables use the codes. Two constraints apply throughout. First, only the direction of an effect is comparable across platforms. Milk, plasma, and the two VAMS matrices were measured on different instruments with different normalizations, so their intensities do not share a scale, and every cross-compartment comparison concerns the sign (up or down) of the within-dataset intervention effect, never its size. Second, these analyses are exploratory. They are based on the covariate-adjusted TMLE models (unadjusted models were kept as a sensitivity analysis), and the tables show the adjusted results. It counts group-level persistence and emergence and does not show accumulation within individuals. 10.2 Cross-compartment concordance of BEP-responsive features We tested whether BEP-responsive features changed in the same direction in different compartments. For each compartment pair (a directed comparison such as milk → maternal plasma) and contrast, we matched features across datasets and measured concordance at a nominal significance threshold and with threshold-free methods: rank–rank hypergeometric overlap (RRHO), weighted correlation, directional GSEA, and a sign test of the second dataset’s direction among the features nominally significant (P < 0.05) in the first. Features were matched across platforms by accurate mass within ionization mode only, using a tolerance for comparing two measured masses, \[\text{ppm} = \frac{|m_1 - m_2|}{m}\times 10^{6} \le 25,\] where both masses are measured, so there is no theoretical or reference mass in the denominator. Retention time (RT) was optional and not used in the initial match. RT was not required because the platforms use different chromatography; RT is used only as supporting evidence for the carnitine annotation (§10.4). A ±25 ppm match without RT on untargeted data can pair isobaric but chemically distinct features, so it generates hypotheses and does not show that two features are the same molecule. Every cross-platform, mass-only match here is therefore putative until confirmed by MS/MS annotation. Reliability of matches. Three kinds of cross-dataset match appear in this section, in decreasing reliability: (1) a shared feature identifier, between maternal and infant postnatal VAMS, which use one feature catalogue; (2) an accurate-mass match between datasets run on the same chromatography (e.g. milk, plasma, prenatal VAMS), where a ±25 ppm match performs well; and (3) an accurate-mass match across chromatography (anything matched to postnatal VAMS from another platform), where compound identity is uncertain and needs annotation. Matches of the third kind are candidates to confirm, not established identities. Interpretation. Concordance is strongest between maternal and infant VAMS, which share one feature catalogue, so their agreement (16 of 18 maternally significant features at 5–6 months) compares the same features. Across platforms, concordance among all mass-matched features is near chance. Among features FDR-significant in both datasets, direction agreement is high in the postnatal comparisons with infant blood (100% in all but one comparison, which had two pairs) but lower for plasma–milk pairs (25–90%) and for prenatal-to-birth comparisons (0–71%). The percentages for all mass-matched features are a lower bound, not a biological effect size. Figure. We ran three analyses on the blood and milk feature lists: direction-agnostic Mummichog pathway enrichment, sign tests of pathway direction, and, for the maternal-blood platforms, chemical-class over-representation. They carry different weight. No blood Mummichog pathway survived FDR correction. In the adjusted models the blood pathway with the lowest FDR was androgen and estrogen biosynthesis and metabolism (raw P ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁴, Q ≈ 0.06), and every other pathway had a higher Q. The pathway grid below therefore gives directional support only. The FDR-significant maternal-blood result is at the level of chemical class. Among BEP-responsive features, maternal plasma showed enrichment of oxylipins (Q ≈ 0.005) and free fatty acids and conjugates (Q ≈ 0.005) among up-regulated features and of acylcarnitines among down-regulated features (Q ≈ 0.03). Maternal postnatal VAMS showed phosphoethanolamines enriched among up-regulated features (Q ≈ 0.03) and diglycerides among down-regulated features (Q ≈ 0.02). The sign tests link these results. De novo fatty-acid biosynthesis and related lipid pathways were decreased in milk but increased in maternal blood at all three milk time points. This pattern is consistent with, but does not demonstrate, a shift from de novo milk-fat synthesis toward circulating or dietary fat (with raised oxylipins and free fatty acids). The Mummichog grid points the same way but does not reach FDR significance on its own. Figure. Left: pathway enrichment, milk vs. maternal blood (adjusted). Right: signed-direction heatmap, with milk lipid pathways down (negative) and maternal-blood lipid pathways up (positive). The tables below give chemical-class over-representation among BEP-responsive maternal-blood features, first regardless of direction and then split into up- and down-regulated features. Unlike the Mummichog grid, these class-level results survive multiple-testing correction in blood; the FDR-significant classes are listed above. Figure. Chemical-class over-representation among BEP-responsive blood features. Maternal plasma: oxylipins and free fatty acids enriched up, acylcarnitines enriched down; maternal postnatal VAMS: phosphoethanolamines up, diglycerides down (all FDR < 0.05). No blood-compartment Mummichog pathway reached FDR significance in the adjusted models (0 of 1,190 pathway–stratum rows at Q < 0.05); the lowest-FDR pathway is Androgen and estrogen biosynthesis and metabolism (Q ≈ 0.06). The FDR-significant blood result is the chemical-class enrichment above, and the sign tests below give the direction of pathway effects. The 40 rows with the lowest P are shown. 10.7 Putative annotation of FDR-significant features The metabolomic platforms are untargeted, so FDR-significant features have only putative annotations, assigned by accurate mass against reference libraries (MSI level ≈ 3); most features return several candidates or none. The tables below list the mass-based candidate annotations for FDR-significant blood and milk features. The curated milk list includes ~48 named metabolites (e.g. pantothenate/B5, ascorbate, fumarate). All names are provisional. The final milk annotation, covering all 1,034 FDR-significant untargeted milk features with counts of named and unresolved features by direction and ionization mode, is in the feature-level putative annotation subsection of §9. The interactive feature map below plots the m/z of each FDR-significant milk feature against its standardized effect, colored by direction. Selecting a mass region (Plotly Box Select) or using the dropdowns filters the annotation table to those features and their putative names. visit contrast direction mode The complete annotation table (all columns, searchable) is below. 10.8 Are the increased features components of the BEP product itself? We checked whether the BEP-up features are high-abundance components of the BEP product passing directly into milk or blood. When each compartment’s up-regulated features were compared with the supplement composition, 1 of 15 BEP-up maternal features and 0 of 11 BEP-up infant features were high-abundance product components, neither above the ~3% background rate expected by chance. The m/z 286.202 acylcarnitine is absent from the product (the nearest product feature in that mass region is ~35 ppm away and is itself depleted), and a medium-chain acylcarnitine of this mass would be an endogenous fatty-acid-oxidation intermediate rather than a listed ingredient. The most likely explanation is therefore an endogenous metabolic response to treatment rather than direct dietary passage of a supplement ingredient, with the product plausibly supplying substrate (fatty acids and amino-acid precursors) rather than the metabolite itself. The concordant increase of this feature in milk and infant blood is consistent with, but does not demonstrate, milk-mediated transfer. Caveat. A weak direct-passage component is not fully excluded. Supplement-abundant features are modestly over-represented among BEP-up maternal plasma features (Fisher P ≈ 3×10⁻⁴ in the tracer table below, vs. P ≈ 0.22 in milk), and one maternal feature is strongly supplement-abundant, making it a candidate for direct dietary passage that merits annotation. The absence of the acylcarnitine from the product is well supported, but extending the endogenous explanation to all increased features awaits MS/MS annotation of these cross-platform matches. 10.9 Infant growth (negative control) As a negative control, we tested whether the increased infant carnitine features were associated with infant growth at 6 months. They were not, so a concordant increase in individual features across milk and infant blood can occur without any downstream growth effect. Figure.
